identity.imageAlt: Pigeon Pea flowers, pods and peas
identity.identityStatement: A productive legume shrub used for food, propagation, biomass and support within warm-climate food forests.

nodes.title: Food Forest
nodes.body: Pigeon pea can combine a harvestable crop with fast biomass, temporary shelter and a productive shrub layer. Its actual role should be read from the plant, season and neighbouring species in the place.
nodes.question: Where does this plant fit into the broader living system?

nodes.title: Uses
nodes.body: Follow the plant from tender pod to green seed, mature dry pulse, leafy fodder and woody stem. Each use belongs to a different harvest stage, and food uses require correct identification and appropriate cooking.
nodes.question: What can people do, make or participate in with this plant?

nodes.title: Propagation
nodes.body: Seed propagation connects plant identity with a particular season and place. Keep source, variety, harvest and performance notes so each new generation retains useful context.
nodes.question: How can people create new plants?

nodes.title: Scientific Information
nodes.body: Scientific information supports reliable identification and comparison. Use botanical name, family, growth form, leaves, flowers and pods together rather than depending on one feature.
nodes.question: What is scientifically established about this plant?

nodes.title: Historical Data
nodes.body: Historical records should keep places, dates, communities and sources visible. They explain how a plant and its practices moved without presenting one simplified origin story as complete.
nodes.question: What has been documented about this plant through time?

nodes.title: Cultivation
nodes.body: Cultivation guidance becomes useful when it is tested against local light, soil, rainfall, season and plant condition. Record responses so care can change with the place.
nodes.question: How does this plant grow, and how can people responsibly support it?

nodes.title: Ecological functions
nodes.body: Explore how roots, canopy, flowers and prunings interact with the surrounding planting. These are relationships to observe and manage, not automatic benefits.

nodes.title: Nitrogen fixation
nodes.body: Pigeon pea can fix atmospheric nitrogen through compatible root bacteria. Much of that nitrogen may leave in harvested seed; neighbours do not receive an instant fertilizer dose. Roots, leaf fall and returned prunings contribute over time as material decomposes.

nodes.title: Root-nodule symbiosis
nodes.body: Root nodules are the visible structures associated with this plant-bacteria relationship. Local observation should be used before assuming that nodulation is active in a particular soil.

nodes.title: Biomass and mulch
nodes.body: Pruned leaves and small stems can be returned to the soil surface as chop-and-drop material.

nodes.title: Nurse plant
nodes.body: Its quick growth can provide temporary shelter and light shade while slower food-forest plants establish.

nodes.title: Flower visitors
nodes.body: Pigeon pea flowers can be visited by bees and other insects. Watch actual visitors at this site, and compare flowering dates with neighbouring plants; a flower is a resource only when a visitor can reach it at the right time.

nodes.title: Habitat structure
nodes.preview: Branching shelter in the shrub layer
nodes.body: The branching canopy can add temporary structure for small garden life. Observe what uses the plant and avoid claiming a relationship that has not been seen locally.

nodes.title: Food-forest layer
nodes.body: Pigeon pea usually occupies the productive shrub layer rather than the permanent canopy. Its branching form can shelter young plants, but its shade and root competition change as it grows; watch the neighbours before deciding how long to keep it.

nodes.title: Shrub layer
nodes.body: Pigeon pea is commonly managed as a shrub or short-lived small tree in a layered planting.

nodes.title: Culinary
nodes.preview: Fresh peas, young pods and dried pulse
nodes.body: Different harvest stages have different textures, cooking needs and cultural uses. Retain the recipe source and preparation context with a food record.

nodes.title: Fresh peas
nodes.body: Shell green, developed seeds before the pod dries and cook them as a fresh legume. Their tender texture suits stews, curries and vegetable dishes; record the cultivar and recipe because cooking time changes with maturity.

nodes.title: Young pods
nodes.body: Very young pods may be cooked before the seeds are prominent. Once fibrous, the pod is not the same vegetable: leave it to develop green seeds or a dry pulse instead.
nodes.safetyNote: Correct identification and appropriate food preparation are required.

nodes.title: Dried pulse
nodes.body: Let pods mature and dry, then shell, sort and store the seeds. Whole dried pigeon pea and split, dehulled dhal are different kitchen forms; both need suitable cooking before serving.

nodes.title: Soak and cook
nodes.body: Inspect and rinse dry seed, soak where the recipe calls for it, discard the soaking water if that is the chosen method, and cook thoroughly until the pulse is tender. Storage age, whole versus split form and altitude change the time required.
nodes.safetyNote: Do not treat raw dried seed as ready-to-eat food.

nodes.title: Culinary record
nodes.body: Record whether the harvest was a young pod, green seed or mature dry pulse, together with the preparation method and the person, publication or tradition that supplied it.
nodes.attribution: A named recipe source, knowledge holder or community should accompany a specific preparation.

nodes.title: Medicinal
nodes.body: Medicinal information belongs here only when it is accurately attributed to a named community, practitioner or reliable source.
nodes.attribution: No universal medicinal claim is made by this reference profile.
nodes.safetyNote: This profile does not provide medical advice.

nodes.title: Traditional knowledge boundary
nodes.body: Record who shared the knowledge, the region and cultural context, and any limits placed on sharing it.
nodes.attribution: A specific knowledge holder or community must be named before adding a practice.
nodes.safetyNote: Traditional-use records are not medical advice.

nodes.title: Craft
nodes.body: Older stems offer short-lived stakes, light woven material and fuel. Select material by strength and intended lifetime; do not treat the soft new growth like finished timber.

nodes.title: Garden stakes
nodes.body: Mature woody stems can be reused as short-lived garden stakes or light structural material.

nodes.title: Basket materials
nodes.body: Flexible material may be tested in locally appropriate craft work. Suitability varies with stem age and preparation.

nodes.title: Fuelwood
nodes.body: Dry woody material may be used as small fuel where local fire rules and clean-burning practices allow.
nodes.safetyNote: Follow local fire restrictions and ventilation requirements.

nodes.title: Animal fodder
nodes.body: Pigeon pea foliage and seed are used in some animal-feeding systems. Species, ration balance and local husbandry guidance matter.
nodes.safetyNote: Confirm suitability and ration guidance for the animal species.

nodes.title: Seed
nodes.body: Seed is the usual way to establish pigeon pea. Preserve the seed line, harvest year and growing conditions alongside the seed, because that context is as valuable as the seed itself.

nodes.title: Direct sowing
nodes.body: Direct sowing avoids transplant disturbance and is useful when the final planting position is ready.

nodes.title: Establishment timing
nodes.body: Choose a warm establishment period with enough soil moisture for germination, adjusting timing to the local climate and season.
nodes.climateContext: Timing varies by climate and season.

nodes.title: Nursery sowing
nodes.body: Seed can also be started in a nursery container and planted out while young, before roots become restricted.

nodes.title: Seed saving
nodes.body: Allow selected pods to mature and dry fully before shelling and storing the seed.

nodes.title: Storage check
nodes.body: Store clean dry seed in a labelled container and review it periodically for moisture or insect damage.

nodes.title: Germination check
nodes.body: Before relying on older stored seed, trial a small counted sample and record how many emerge. Keep the date and conditions with the result.

nodes.title: Sharing seed
nodes.body: Record the variety, source, harvest season and local performance when sharing seed so future growers retain useful context.

nodes.title: Taxonomy
nodes.body: The accepted name Cajanus cajan places this plant in Fabaceae. A common name alone is not enough for confident identification or for linking a local record to a scientific reference.

nodes.title: Accepted botanical name
nodes.body: The botanical name used in this reference profile is Cajanus cajan.

nodes.title: Taxonomic record
nodes.body: Taxonomic names and synonymy should be checked against a current botanical authority before formal publication.

nodes.title: Family
nodes.body: Pigeon pea belongs to the legume family, Fabaceae.

nodes.title: Morphology
nodes.body: Read leaves, pea-shaped flowers, branching habit and pods together. One feature may vary with variety, age or growing conditions, while the combination gives a more dependable identification.

nodes.title: Growth form
nodes.body: It is a branching, often short-lived perennial shrub that can become a small tree under favourable management.

nodes.title: Leaves
nodes.body: The leaves are typically divided into three leaflets. Leaf form should be checked alongside flowers, pods, branching and a reliable local identification reference.

nodes.title: Flowers
nodes.body: Flowers have the characteristic pea-family form and may show colour variation. Record colour and flowering time as supporting features rather than using them alone.

nodes.title: Pods and seed
nodes.preview: Flattened pods with visible seed positions
nodes.body: Pods mature from green to dry and contain several seeds. Pod shape, surface, colour and seed appearance can support identification and harvest records.

nodes.title: Phenology
nodes.body: Flowering and pod production respond to variety, day length, temperature, water and plant age.

nodes.title: Common names
nodes.body: Pigeon pea has many regional names. Attach a language, place and contributor to any added name so a shared word does not silently erase local meaning.

nodes.title: Pigeon pea
nodes.body: Pigeon pea is the primary common name used in this reference profile. Use this menu to add regional names with their language, place and source.

nodes.title: Range and movement
nodes.body: The plant is cultivated across warm regions, but origin, domestication and later movement are different questions. Keep a dated source with each historical claim.

nodes.title: Native range
nodes.body: Published accounts of origin and early domestication should be retained with their sources because historical interpretations can differ.

nodes.title: Cultivated distribution
nodes.body: Pigeon pea is cultivated across many tropical and subtropical regions for food, fodder and farming-system functions.

nodes.title: Regional movement record
nodes.body: A useful movement record names the place, approximate date, variety or seed line, people or organisation involved, and documentary source.

nodes.title: Local introduction record
nodes.preview: How did this seed reach this place?
nodes.body: For a project record, note who introduced the seed, when it arrived, where it came from and whether the current plants descend from that material.

nodes.title: Cultural history
nodes.body: Food preparations and growing practices have long histories in different communities. Add specific stories with their knowledge holders and permissions, rather than presenting one practice as universal.

nodes.title: Attributed traditional knowledge
nodes.body: Traditional knowledge must be presented with appropriate attribution and must not be framed as universally shared knowledge.
nodes.attribution: A named knowledge holder or community is required.

nodes.title: Climate
nodes.body: Pigeon pea is a warm-season plant. Its flowering, survival and length of production depend on local temperatures, day length, rainfall and the variety planted.

nodes.title: Warm growing conditions
nodes.body: Growth is strongest in warm conditions. Local frost exposure, rainfall pattern and planting season should guide management.
nodes.climateContext: Local climate and season change results.

nodes.title: Seasonal variation
nodes.body: Record flowering, pod set, dieback and regrowth by season rather than assuming the same cycle in every region.

nodes.title: Light
nodes.body: Give the plant enough direct light for sturdy growth and pod set. Also measure the light it removes from younger neighbours as its crown expands.

nodes.title: Full sun
nodes.body: Full sun generally supports strong flowering and pod production, while neighbouring canopy growth can change performance.

nodes.title: Spacing and access
nodes.body: Allow enough room to reach the plant for pruning and harvest while considering shade on neighbours. The useful spacing depends on the intended size and pruning cycle.

nodes.title: Soil
nodes.body: Drainage and active soil biology matter for establishment and nodulation. The plant may tolerate relatively poor soils, but poor growth should prompt observation, not an assumption that nitrogen fixation will solve everything.

nodes.title: Soil drainage
nodes.body: Establishment is generally more reliable in soil that drains after heavy rain.

nodes.title: Soil observation
nodes.body: Observe drainage after rain, root health and whether nodules are present before assuming the soil relationship is functioning. Add dated photographs or notes when possible.

nodes.title: Water
nodes.body: New seedlings need moisture to establish. Older plants can use deeper soil water, yet prolonged drought can still reduce growth and pod yield.

nodes.title: Establishment water
nodes.body: Provide suitable moisture during germination and early establishment, then adapt watering to soil, rainfall, season and plant condition.

nodes.title: Maintenance
nodes.body: Manage this short-lived shrub for the job it is doing: harvest, living shelter, mulch or seed. Pruning, health checks and eventual replacement all change the surrounding planting.

nodes.title: Pruning
nodes.body: Pruning can manage height, light and biomass production. Timing and severity should reflect plant health and the needs of neighbouring plants.

nodes.title: Chop-and-drop cycle
nodes.body: Place clean, suitable prunings on the soil surface while keeping material away from vulnerable stems and avoiding diseased material.

nodes.title: Regrowth response
nodes.body: Note the cut height, season, plant condition and time taken to regrow. This helps refine a pruning cycle for biomass, light or harvest rather than repeating a fixed schedule.

nodes.title: Plant health check
nodes.body: Record the location and timing of leaf damage, stem problems, pests or dieback together with recent weather and management. Compare change over time before selecting a treatment.

nodes.title: Harvest
nodes.body: Harvest timing depends on whether tender seed, young pods or mature dry pulse is wanted.

nodes.title: Where nitrogen goes
nodes.body: Fixation supports the pigeon pea plant first. Nitrogen exported in seed is removed from the site; nitrogen in roots, fallen leaves and returned prunings may become available after decomposition. Compare a harvested-and-cleared plant with one whose residues remain.

nodes.title: Nodule field check
nodes.body: With permission, inspect a small root sample from a representative plant. Record whether nodules are present and the plant’s condition; nodule presence alone does not measure a nitrogen-fixation rate.

nodes.title: Flower to pod
nodes.body: Record flowering dates, insect visits and later pod set on the same branches. This can reveal local patterns without claiming that one visitor caused every pod.

nodes.title: Roots and soil
nodes.body: The root system can explore deeper soil and help create channels as roots grow and decay. Soil texture, compaction and moisture determine what this means in a particular bed.

nodes.title: Companion light window
nodes.body: Use the young shrub for temporary shelter, then check whether its canopy is beginning to suppress the intended long-term crop. Prune or replace it according to observed light and growth, not a fixed calendar.

nodes.title: Three harvest stages
nodes.body: The tender pod, shelled green seed and fully dry seed are three distinct ingredients. Label each harvest stage before choosing a recipe so the preparation matches the texture.

nodes.title: Green-seed dishes
nodes.body: Cook shelled green pigeon peas in a stew, curry or vegetable dish where they retain some shape. Taste for tenderness and record the household or published recipe that guided the preparation.

nodes.title: Tender-pod dishes
nodes.body: Select very young pods with little developed seed, trim and cook according to a trusted local recipe. Test tenderness first; mature pods are better treated as a seed harvest.

nodes.title: Split dhal
nodes.body: Dried pigeon pea may be dehulled and split for dhal. The split form cooks differently from the whole seed and is used in soups, dals and other regional dishes; retain the named recipe tradition.

nodes.title: Food storage
nodes.body: Dry shelled seed thoroughly, remove damaged seed, and store it clean and labelled in a pest-resistant container. Recheck for moisture or insects before cooking.

nodes.title: Leafy fodder
nodes.body: Leaves and tender stems may be used as forage in some livestock systems. Their share of a ration should be decided with species-specific feeding guidance, not inferred from human food uses.
nodes.safetyNote: Do not use as a sole feed or assume suitability for every animal.

nodes.title: Seedling stage
nodes.body: Mark the sowing position and keep competing growth from overwhelming small seedlings. Record emergence, insect damage and moisture so later performance has an understandable starting point.

nodes.title: Pod and seed count
nodes.body: Count seeds in several mature pods and photograph their shape and colour. Variation within a plant is normal; use this as a supporting record rather than a single-feature identification test.

nodes.title: Flowering calendar
nodes.body: Record the first flowers, peak flowering, first green pods and dry-pod harvest. Comparing years can reveal a variety’s response to day length, rainfall or pruning at this site.

nodes.title: After harvest
nodes.body: After a pulse harvest, decide whether healthy stems and foliage will become mulch, stakes or be removed. This choice changes how much plant material stays in the food-forest system.

nodes.title: Orchard-edge shelter trial
nodes.preview: Test temporary shelter beside young trees
nodes.body: Permaculture growers describe using pigeon pea beside young fruit trees or on a field edge as a temporary shelter plant. Treat this as a design example: record distance, shade, water, pruning and the fruit tree response, then thin or remove pigeon pea if it competes with the long-term tree.

nodes.title: Living hedge example
nodes.body: Some warm-climate permaculture systems use pigeon pea as a productive hedge or windbreak. Its useful life, density and wind protection vary with site and management; observe gaps, shade, wind exposure and neighbour competition before relying on it as a barrier.

nodes.title: Intercrop light check
nodes.body: Pigeon pea is used in some alley and mixed-crop designs. Before adding an understory or crop between rows, track sun and shade at different times and seasons, soil moisture and access for harvest; a useful layer in one climate can compete in another.

nodes.title: Trellis trial
nodes.body: A pigeon-pea shrub may be used as a support in some mixed plantings, but its branches are not a guaranteed trellis. Trial only with a light, non-damaging climber; observe branch strength, airflow, harvest access and whether the climber suppresses the shrub.

nodes.title: Replacement window
nodes.preview: Plan the next layer before decline
nodes.body: Pigeon pea may be short-lived compared with fruit trees and other permanent food-forest plants. Record vigour, useful function, seed production and neighbour growth so replacement planting can be timed for this site instead of relying on a fixed lifespan.
